title: [Devlog] How I used LLMs to build "Sweden Cargo" — a 3D articulated truck simulator running purely in Three.js
author: Ali_wan
selftext:
>Hey r/aigamedev,  
>  
>I wanted to share a breakdown of a browser game I recently developed called **Sweden Cargo** (playable clip above).  
>  
>It’s a 3D truck-driving simulator where you haul fragile freight from Stockholm across Swedish cities (Linköping, Göteborg, Malmö, etc.) through procedural pine forests, lakes, and highway curves.  
>  
>The core game was architected and built with LLM-assisted prompting (iterative workflows in Claude), and I wanted to share what worked, where the AI struggled, and how we solved it:  
>  
>  
>  
>Simulating an articulated Scania box truck with a drawbar trailer in lightweight WebGL without heavy third-party physics engines was a massive challenge.  
>  
>  
>  
>I wanted zero load times and no external 100MB asset downloads:  
>  
>  
>  
>Cargo isn't just static score; more fragile cargo (glass/electronics) takes higher damage from harsh steering, guardrail scraping, and high-speed cornering. AI was great at quickly structuring the state machine for depot loading (docking in green zones, opening/closing the rear gates with `O`), route timers, and the garage progression.  
>  
>  
>  
>LLMs are incredible for rapid mathematical prototyping in Three.js (vector projections, curve math, and shader tints), but tuning the actual *game feel* (weight of the truck, braking curve, camera lerping) still requires tight human steering and constant hands-on playtesting.  
>  
>🔗 **Live Game (No download/login, works on PC & mobile):**  
[https://ibuerte.com/games/sweden-cargo/](https://ibuerte.com/games/sweden-cargo/)  
>  
>Video attached shows the cockpit & chase camera handling the Swedish motorway. Happy to answer questions about the prompt workflow or the Three.js math!
